claims.text: The as-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a homogeneous FCC matrix.
The as-built alloy has minimal pre-existing oxide content.
Temperatures above approximately 600°C provide sufficient diffusion kinetics for selective oxidation in this alloy.
Grain boundaries are preferential sites for oxidation in this alloy.
Al and Ti diffuse to grain boundaries and oxidize preferentially under elevated-temperature oxidizing conditions.
Preferential oxidation depletes Al and Ti near the grain boundaries.
Selective oxidation produces discontinuous Al2O3 and TiO2 precipitates at grain boundaries.
The grain-boundary oxide phases are brittle and non-protective.
The grain-boundary oxides compromise intergranular cohesion.
Thermal stresses cause the oxide phases to spall.
Oxide spallation creates stress concentrations and microcracks.
Spallation-induced microcracks coalesce and cause rapid degradation and catastrophic mechanical failure.
A reducing H2/N2 environment suppresses selective oxidation and preserves alloy integrity relative to an oxidizing environment.
After exposure near 700°C for 100 hours, oxidizing-atmosphere specimens will have more isolated grain-boundary oxide precipitates, oxide spallation, and surface roughness than the as-built baseline.
Oxidizing-atmosphere specimens will have lower mechanical strength and earlier failure under load than the as-built baseline.
Reducing-atmosphere specimens will retain a more continuous, protective surface and degrade more slowly than oxidizing-atmosphere specimens.
The proposed mechanism may not operate at lower temperatures or during exposures too short to form appreciable oxide.

The hypothesis is falsified if oxidizing and reducing exposures show no statistically significant difference in grain-boundary oxidation, spallation, and associated mechanical degradation, or if catastrophic failure occurs without observable selective grain-boundary oxidation.
